<reason>Exceptionally close, high-quality debate that narrowed cleanly to one question: does the obligation extend to a public, kin-witnessed ceremony, or only to the promise itself? A's severability thesis (form vs. invoice) survived B's best attack—the "when's the actual wedding?" lived-enforcement critique—and A turned the premise around: tradition is the cheapest defense against the very market/feed forces B's own opening blamed for performance pressure. A answered both pressure questions with concrete commitments (a costly kin-facing ceremony; the eloper's sting as declined witness, not missing sparklers), exposing a real wobble in B's residuals (B2.5's "owe their community a promise" collapsed into B4.3's elopement-pays-the-debt). B's Q1 trap and closing catch ("that is my standard, not theirs") were genuinely damaging, but A's closing answered with the rule-level/act-level distinction and "the form is the cap." B's promise/performance fork never squarely engaged A's witness-vs-spectator distinction, and B's R2 claim of "silence on both" was chronologically cheap—A had not yet had a turn to answer. A made the debate slightly easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pressure-question chain decided it: B's Q1 demanded one costly, onlooker-serving obligation; A answered directly (kin-attended ceremony despite airfare) and defended the sting as witness-policing, not chair-policing; B's closing reframed that as a concession of the "earned" standard, but A's final speech neutralized it—inheritance is how functional institutions bind without each couple re-running the cost-benefit check—while B never answered why elopement satisfies "owing the community a promise."</best_rebuttal>
